newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: FORGED TICKETS MAY HAVE PROMPTED SOCCER STADIUM DEATHS.
newsitem.headline: FORGED TICKETS MAY HAVE PROMPTED SOCCER STADIUM DEATHS.

text.p: Forged tickets may have prompted a stampede that led to the deaths of at least 79 fans in an overcrowded stadium at a World Cup match, soccer's governing body FIFA suggested on Thursday.

An avalanche of fans tumbled down the concrete steps which serve as seats in the Mateo Flores stadium in Guatemala City as others poured in to watch Wednesday's international between Guatemala and Costa Rica.
Guatemalan officials said the stadium was packed well beyond its 45,800 capacity an hour before kickoff with some suggestions that up to 60,000 were in the ground.
FIFA said in Zurich, Switzerland, that a preliminary report submitted by their match commissioner Arnoldo Levinson of Mexico spoke of forged tickets being sold before the game.
The report said angry fans kicked down an entrance door to the south stands causing spectators already inside to cascade down to the lower levels.
The report noted that security personnel opened emergency gates to the pitch but could not relieve the crush.
The exact cause of the disaster will be investigated by Guatemalan goverment authorities, which FIFA said were responsible for safety inside and outside the stadium.
Guatemala president Alvaro Arzu, who addressed the crowd from the pitch with tears in his eyes, declared a three-day period of national mourning.
A Reuters correspondent counted 79 dead, including two children, while local radio stations reported more than 80 fatalities and at least 150 injured.
Dead bodies were lined up in a row on the athletics track surrounding the pitch and covered with blankets as emergency services tried to revive suffocation victims and ferry the injured to hospital.
Some fans tried to perform mouth-to-mouth resuscitation on victims, helping about 15 overwhelmed firefighters.
Both Arzu and Costa Roca president Jose Maria Figueres were scheduled to attend the game but neither was in the stadium at the time of the incident.
Guatemala's attorney general, solicitor general and health minister all made public calls for a thorough investigation to determine who was responsible.

It was the worst stadium disaster in World Cup history and one of the worst ever in soccer, recalling the 1989 tragedy at Hillsborough in the English city of Sheffield when 95 fans died in similar circumstances.

FIFA spokesman Andreas Herren would not confirm that FIFA would conduct its own investigation. But he said: "These are matters that cannot be discussed but the media can draw their obvious conclusions."
If found guilty of negligence in the disaster the Guatemala football association could face possible FIFA sanctions.
The match has been postponed until further notice.
"With the current situation that is not the main concern at the moment," said Herren. "We must first respect the victims of this tragedy."
The Mateo Flores stadium is a concrete bowl on the outskirts of Guatemala City which serves as both the national stadium and the venue of the capital's leading soccer clubs.
Briton Simon Inglis, an expert who has written several books on soccer stadiums, said: "It was a classic soccer stadium disaster. They nearly all happen on entry or exit from the ground.
"In this stadium there are no numbered seats and spectators sit on concrete terraces. It makes crowd control very difficult."
